112:Existing tools address only fragments of this problem: \texttt{tiktoken}~\cite{sennrich2016bpe} and Anthropic's tokenizer provide offline token counts but have no IDE integration, no multi-provider support, and no cost modeling. Bergemann et al.~\cite{bergemann2025economics} introduced a Cobb–Douglas production function framework for LLM economics but did not implement a developer-facing tool. Without integrated tooling, three compounding problems arise:
115:  \item \textit{Attention dilution}: irrelevant files compete with relevant ones for the limited context window, degrading model output quality~\cite{bergemann2025economics,hong2025contextrot}.
117:  \item \textit{Context rot}: after 20+ turns, stale context introduces inconsistencies; Hong et al.~\cite{hong2025contextrot} demonstrated that this degradation occurs non-uniformly across models, even on simple retrieval tasks, and worsens with distractor content.

Now I have a complete picture of the entire file. Here is the full report of every sizing problem found, organized by category.

---

## Sizing Problems in `/Users/vfaraji89/Documents/contribuet-github/tokalator/paper/paper.txt`

The document class is `cas-dc` (two-column A4). Full text width is approximately 17 cm; single-column width is approximately 8.3 cm.

---

### 1. Tables with Hardcoded Absolute Column Widths (`p{Ncm}`)

**Line 152 — `executabelMetadata` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l p{4.2cm} p{8.5cm} @{}}
```
Two absolute-width `p{}` columns: `p{4.2cm}` and `p{8.5cm}`. Their sum (12.7 cm) plus the leading `l` column fills the two-column span very tightly. If any internal table font or margin changes, overflow is immediate. Should use relative widths tied to `\linewidth` (e.g., `p{0.25\linewidth}` and `p{0.50\linewidth}`).

---

**Lines 941 — `tab:tests` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|p{0.8cm}|p{3.5cm}|}
```
`p{0.8cm}` for the "Tests" count column is very narrow — only 8 mm. Three-digit numbers or bold text can overflow it. `p{3.5cm}` for "Coverage" is also hardcoded. Neither is relative.

---

**Line 977 — `tab:commands` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{|l|p{7.5cm}|}
```
`p{7.5cm}` is hardcoded. In the `table*` (full text width ~17 cm), the command-name `l` column will consume additional space, which is unconstrained. The hardcoded 7.5 cm is not portable across layout changes.

---

**Line 1296 — `tab:survey-instrument` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} c p{9.8cm} c c @{}}
```
`p{9.8cm}` is hardcoded. With two `c` columns on each side plus the `p{}` column, the total can approach or exceed the full text width depending on how wide the `c` columns become.

---

**Lines 1659 — `tab:survey-results` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c p{3.6cm} p{4.4cm} @{}}
```
Two hardcoded `p{}` columns: `p{3.6cm}` and `p{4.4cm}`. Total of those two alone is 8 cm. Combined with the `l` and two `c` columns, the total is approximately 12–13 cm in a 17 cm span. This is borderline and not robust to font or margin changes.

---

### 2. Tables with Many Columns and No Width Constraints

**Line 184 — `tab:comparison` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c c c c c c @{}}
```
8 columns, all auto-width (`l` and 7 `c`). The `l` column contains text like "Chat participant / slash cmds" and "Conversation cost projection". The column headers span two physical rows (lines 186–187) using a two-row `\textbf{}` structure. There is no `\resizebox`, no `\scalebox`, and no `p{}` width on the feature-name column to control wrapping. With 8 columns squeezed across the full text width, the feature-description column will be given an unconstrained natural width, and the table is likely to overflow.

---

**Line 1558 — `tab:survey-distributions` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c c c c c c @{}}
```
8 columns again. The `l` column contains verbose strings like "Q1: \texttt{/preview} usefulness" and "Q5: \texttt{/compaction} usefulness". The 6 `c` columns (ratings 1–5, Mean, SD) have no width specification. TeX will auto-size the `l` column to its natural width and then try to fit 6 more `c` columns alongside it. There is no `\resizebox` guard.

---

**Line 1709 — `tab:billing-full` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l r r r r @{}}
```
6 columns, two of which are unconstrained `l`. The second `l` column (Product / SKU) contains strings of very different lengths, the shortest being "Copilot premium request" and the longest being "Actions Linux (CodeQL + Dependabot + Pages + ci.yml)" (line 1729, 52 characters). The longest string will set the column width for all rows, and with four more `r` columns after it, the table risks overflowing the full text width. No `\resizebox` is present.

---

**Lines 1639 — `tab:survey-gender` (`\begin{table}` — single column)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c c @{}}
```
4 columns inside a single-column `\begin{table}` (single-column float; column width ~8.3 cm). The header row (line 1641) is:
```
\textbf{Item} & \textbf{\hl{Female} ($n=13$)} & \textbf{\hl{Male} ($n=35$)} & \textbf{\hl{N-B/Undisc.} ($n=2$)}
```
The three header cells alone ("Female (n=13)", "Male (n=35)", "N-B/Undisc. (n=2)") in three `c` columns plus the "Item" `l` column will expand well beyond 8.3 cm. This table will overflow the single column. It should either be promoted to `\begin{table*}` or have its columns constrained with `p{}`.

---

### 3. Tables Using `\begin{table}` Instead of `\begin{table*}` with Potentially Wide Content

**Line 699 — `tab:billing-summary` (`\begin{table}` — single column)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l r @{}}
```
Two columns, `l` and `r`. The `l` column contains entries such as:
- Line 715: "Intensive sprint (Feb~6--11)" 
- Line 716: "Long-tail development (Feb~12--Mar~7)"

The `r` column for those same rows contains:
- "911 requests (64.5\%), \$25.00 net"
- "502 requests (35.5\%), \$3.36 net"

These right-column cells are very long and will be placed in a single `r` column with no wrapping (unconstrained width), in a single-column float (~8.3 cm wide). The table will overflow. Using `\begin{table*}` or constraining the `r` column with `p{}` would fix this.

---

### 4. TikZ Figures with Hardcoded Dimensions That May Not Scale

**Lines 276–393 — `fig:seq` (sequence diagram, `\begin{figure*}`)**

This is the most severe sizing problem in the file:

- Lines 290–294: Actor columns placed at absolute TikZ coordinates `\colA=0`, `\colB=3.0`, `\colC=6.0`, `\colD=9.0`, `\colE=12.0` (all in cm). The last actor box has `minimum width=2.2cm`, making the right edge of the diagram ~14.2 cm wide. This fits within the ~17 cm text width, but barely, and is not adaptive.
- **Line 302: `\def\bottom{-19.0}`** — the diagram's vertical span is 0 to −19.0 cm, plus the bottom actor boxes at `\bottom - 0.5 = -19.5 cm`. With the header actors at y=0 this is a **~20.5 cm tall figure**, taller than an A4 page's text area (~24.7 cm). Combined with the caption, it will essentially fill an entire page.
- No `\resizebox`, no `\scalebox`, no `scale=` option on the `tikzpicture` environment.

---

**Lines 731–788 — `fig:billing-trend` (bar+line chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- **Line 741: `\def\W{19.5}`** — the x-axis is drawn at `(\W,0) = (19.5, 0)`, i.e., **19.5 cm wide**. A4 paper with standard LaTeX margins has a text width of approximately 16.5–17 cm. This TikZ picture is **2.5–3 cm wider than the text width** and will overflow the page boundaries. The right y-axis is placed at x=`\W+0.85 = 20.35 cm`.
- The legend at lines 784–787 also uses absolute coordinates within this 19.5 cm frame.
- No `\resizebox` or `\scalebox` to compensate.

---

**Lines 1048–1158 — `fig:commits` (bar+line chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- **Line 1053: `\def\W{14.5}`** — x-axis spans from 0 to `\W+0.5 = 15.0 cm`. The right y-axis and its label are at `\W = 14.5 cm` and `\W+0.1 / \W+0.85`. Width of ~15 cm fits within the text width of ~17 cm.
- The legend is placed at y=−1.1 to −0.8 (below the x-axis). The x-axis tick labels are rotated 45° (`anchor=north east`) at y=−0.1. The rotated tick labels will extend below y=−0.1, overlapping with or obscuring the legend at y=−1.1. No explicit vertical spacing is allocated between the rotated labels and the legend.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1205–1268 — `fig:testdist` (bar chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- The main y-axis extends to y=7.0 (line 1210), axes extend to x=9.0 (line 1211), but chart bars are positioned up to x=7.8.
- The x-axis labels at y=−0.1 use `\rotatebox{55}` inside `\node[anchor=north east]`. These rotated labels will extend below y=−0.1 with no allocated vertical space, potentially clipping at the figure boundary.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1330–1408 — `fig:survey-demo` (multi-panel bar chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- Panel C's axis runs from x=9.0 to x=13.8 (line 1386). The last bar right edge is at x=13.7, and the right y-axis labels use `anchor=west` at x=8.92 (Panel B) and x=13.8 (Panel C). Total visible extent is ~14 cm plus axis label text extending slightly beyond. This fits within 17 cm but is tight.
- Panel A y-axis labels are placed at x=−0.08 with `anchor=east`, and x-axis labels at y=−0.12 with `anchor=north`. Panel C bars have two-row x-axis labels at y=−0.12 and y=−0.42 (lines 1390–1406), which extend 0.42 cm below the baseline with no reserved space.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1459–1548 — `fig:survey-likert` (horizontal stacked bars, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- Q-labels are placed at x=−0.12 with `anchor=east`, style `qlbl`. Labels like "Q2: Tokenizer acc." and "Q5: \texttt{/compaction}" have non-trivial text widths that extend into negative x territory. TikZ's bounding box for the picture will include this leftward protrusion, which can shift the overall figure placement or cause overflow at the left margin if the figure is already constrained.
- The x-axis extends to x=10.3 (line 1478) and mean-value labels appear at x up to 8.15. Total right extent is ~10.3 cm. With the leftward label protrusion, the effective picture width is ~11–12 cm.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1578–1629 — `fig:survey-means` (horizontal bars, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- Q-labels at x=−0.12 with `anchor=east` (same issue as `fig:survey-likert`): labels like "Q6: Token awareness", "Q8: Install ease", "Q9: Dashboard clarity" extend into negative x space.
- Mean-value labels (`meanlbl` style, `anchor=west`) are placed immediately to the right of each bar end. The widest bar ends at x=8.10 (Q6), and the label "4.50" is at x=8.15. Additional tick labels at x=9.0 are placed at x=9.0 (line 1591). Total right extent ~9.5 cm. Tight but likely OK.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

### 5. Figures Using Suboptimal Relative Sizing

**Line 460 — `fig:dashboard` (`\begin{figure*}`)**
```
\includegraphics[width=0.52\textwidth]{tokalator-ui.png}
```
`0.52\textwidth` in a `figure*` environment means the image occupies only 52% of the full two-column text width, leaving 24% white space on each side after centering. For a screenshot used as a principal software demonstration figure, this will appear noticeably small. Compare to `fig:arch` (line 240, `0.88\textwidth`) and `fig:marketplace` (line 817, `0.92\textwidth`), which are more appropriate. `width=0.75\textwidth` or wider would be more consistent.

---

### 6. Caption Placement Inconsistency (three tables)

In `cas-dc` and most journal styles, table captions are placed **above** the tabular content. The majority of tables in this document follow that convention (captions at lines 150, 182, 702, 1294, 1416, 1637, 1657, 1707). However, three tables have the `\caption`/`\label` placed **after** `\end{tabular}`, producing a caption below the table:

| Table | `\end{tabular}` line | `\caption` line |
|---|---|---|
| `tab:tests` | 963 | 964 |
| `tab:commands` | 1033 | 1034 |
| `tab:codebase` | 1194 | 1195 |

This is not a sizing problem per se, but it is a formatting inconsistency that many journal style files (including `cas-dc`) treat as an error in the context of tables.

Now I have a complete picture of the entire file. Here is the full report of every sizing problem found, organized by category.

---

## Sizing Problems in `/Users/vfaraji89/Documents/contribuet-github/tokalator/paper/paper.txt`

The document class is `cas-dc` (two-column A4). Full text width is approximately 17 cm; single-column width is approximately 8.3 cm.

---

### 1. Tables with Hardcoded Absolute Column Widths (`p{Ncm}`)

**Line 152 — `executabelMetadata` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l p{4.2cm} p{8.5cm} @{}}
```
Two absolute-width `p{}` columns: `p{4.2cm}` and `p{8.5cm}`. Their sum (12.7 cm) plus the leading `l` column fills the two-column span very tightly. If any internal table font or margin changes, overflow is immediate. Should use relative widths tied to `\linewidth` (e.g., `p{0.25\linewidth}` and `p{0.50\linewidth}`).

---

**Lines 941 — `tab:tests` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|p{0.8cm}|p{3.5cm}|}
```
`p{0.8cm}` for the "Tests" count column is very narrow — only 8 mm. Three-digit numbers or bold text can overflow it. `p{3.5cm}` for "Coverage" is also hardcoded. Neither is relative.

---

**Line 977 — `tab:commands` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{|l|p{7.5cm}|}
```
`p{7.5cm}` is hardcoded. In the `table*` (full text width ~17 cm), the command-name `l` column will consume additional space, which is unconstrained. The hardcoded 7.5 cm is not portable across layout changes.

---

**Line 1296 — `tab:survey-instrument` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} c p{9.8cm} c c @{}}
```
`p{9.8cm}` is hardcoded. With two `c` columns on each side plus the `p{}` column, the total can approach or exceed the full text width depending on how wide the `c` columns become.

---

**Lines 1659 — `tab:survey-results` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c p{3.6cm} p{4.4cm} @{}}
```
Two hardcoded `p{}` columns: `p{3.6cm}` and `p{4.4cm}`. Total of those two alone is 8 cm. Combined with the `l` and two `c` columns, the total is approximately 12–13 cm in a 17 cm span. This is borderline and not robust to font or margin changes.

---

### 2. Tables with Many Columns and No Width Constraints

**Line 184 — `tab:comparison` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c c c c c c @{}}
```
8 columns, all auto-width (`l` and 7 `c`). The `l` column contains text like "Chat participant / slash cmds" and "Conversation cost projection". The column headers span two physical rows (lines 186–187) using a two-row `\textbf{}` structure. There is no `\resizebox`, no `\scalebox`, and no `p{}` width on the feature-name column to control wrapping. With 8 columns squeezed across the full text width, the feature-description column will be given an unconstrained natural width, and the table is likely to overflow.

---

**Line 1558 — `tab:survey-distributions` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c c c c c c @{}}
```
8 columns again. The `l` column contains verbose strings like "Q1: \texttt{/preview} usefulness" and "Q5: \texttt{/compaction} usefulness". The 6 `c` columns (ratings 1–5, Mean, SD) have no width specification. TeX will auto-size the `l` column to its natural width and then try to fit 6 more `c` columns alongside it. There is no `\resizebox` guard.

---

**Line 1709 — `tab:billing-full` (`\begin{table*}`)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l r r r r @{}}
```
6 columns, two of which are unconstrained `l`. The second `l` column (Product / SKU) contains strings of very different lengths, the shortest being "Copilot premium request" and the longest being "Actions Linux (CodeQL + Dependabot + Pages + ci.yml)" (line 1729, 52 characters). The longest string will set the column width for all rows, and with four more `r` columns after it, the table risks overflowing the full text width. No `\resizebox` is present.

---

**Lines 1639 — `tab:survey-gender` (`\begin{table}` — single column)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l c c c @{}}
```
4 columns inside a single-column `\begin{table}` (single-column float; column width ~8.3 cm). The header row (line 1641) is:
```
\textbf{Item} & \textbf{\hl{Female} ($n=13$)} & \textbf{\hl{Male} ($n=35$)} & \textbf{\hl{N-B/Undisc.} ($n=2$)}
```
The three header cells alone ("Female (n=13)", "Male (n=35)", "N-B/Undisc. (n=2)") in three `c` columns plus the "Item" `l` column will expand well beyond 8.3 cm. This table will overflow the single column. It should either be promoted to `\begin{table*}` or have its columns constrained with `p{}`.

---

### 3. Tables Using `\begin{table}` Instead of `\begin{table*}` with Potentially Wide Content

**Line 699 — `tab:billing-summary` (`\begin{table}` — single column)**
```
\begin{tabular}{@{} l r @{}}
```
Two columns, `l` and `r`. The `l` column contains entries such as:
- Line 715: "Intensive sprint (Feb~6--11)" 
- Line 716: "Long-tail development (Feb~12--Mar~7)"

The `r` column for those same rows contains:
- "911 requests (64.5\%), \$25.00 net"
- "502 requests (35.5\%), \$3.36 net"

These right-column cells are very long and will be placed in a single `r` column with no wrapping (unconstrained width), in a single-column float (~8.3 cm wide). The table will overflow. Using `\begin{table*}` or constraining the `r` column with `p{}` would fix this.

---

### 4. TikZ Figures with Hardcoded Dimensions That May Not Scale

**Lines 276–393 — `fig:seq` (sequence diagram, `\begin{figure*}`)**

This is the most severe sizing problem in the file:

- Lines 290–294: Actor columns placed at absolute TikZ coordinates `\colA=0`, `\colB=3.0`, `\colC=6.0`, `\colD=9.0`, `\colE=12.0` (all in cm). The last actor box has `minimum width=2.2cm`, making the right edge of the diagram ~14.2 cm wide. This fits within the ~17 cm text width, but barely, and is not adaptive.
- **Line 302: `\def\bottom{-19.0}`** — the diagram's vertical span is 0 to −19.0 cm, plus the bottom actor boxes at `\bottom - 0.5 = -19.5 cm`. With the header actors at y=0 this is a **~20.5 cm tall figure**, taller than an A4 page's text area (~24.7 cm). Combined with the caption, it will essentially fill an entire page.
- No `\resizebox`, no `\scalebox`, no `scale=` option on the `tikzpicture` environment.

---

**Lines 731–788 — `fig:billing-trend` (bar+line chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- **Line 741: `\def\W{19.5}`** — the x-axis is drawn at `(\W,0) = (19.5, 0)`, i.e., **19.5 cm wide**. A4 paper with standard LaTeX margins has a text width of approximately 16.5–17 cm. This TikZ picture is **2.5–3 cm wider than the text width** and will overflow the page boundaries. The right y-axis is placed at x=`\W+0.85 = 20.35 cm`.
- The legend at lines 784–787 also uses absolute coordinates within this 19.5 cm frame.
- No `\resizebox` or `\scalebox` to compensate.

---

**Lines 1048–1158 — `fig:commits` (bar+line chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- **Line 1053: `\def\W{14.5}`** — x-axis spans from 0 to `\W+0.5 = 15.0 cm`. The right y-axis and its label are at `\W = 14.5 cm` and `\W+0.1 / \W+0.85`. Width of ~15 cm fits within the text width of ~17 cm.
- The legend is placed at y=−1.1 to −0.8 (below the x-axis). The x-axis tick labels are rotated 45° (`anchor=north east`) at y=−0.1. The rotated tick labels will extend below y=−0.1, overlapping with or obscuring the legend at y=−1.1. No explicit vertical spacing is allocated between the rotated labels and the legend.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1205–1268 — `fig:testdist` (bar chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- The main y-axis extends to y=7.0 (line 1210), axes extend to x=9.0 (line 1211), but chart bars are positioned up to x=7.8.
- The x-axis labels at y=−0.1 use `\rotatebox{55}` inside `\node[anchor=north east]`. These rotated labels will extend below y=−0.1 with no allocated vertical space, potentially clipping at the figure boundary.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1330–1408 — `fig:survey-demo` (multi-panel bar chart, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- Panel C's axis runs from x=9.0 to x=13.8 (line 1386). The last bar right edge is at x=13.7, and the right y-axis labels use `anchor=west` at x=8.92 (Panel B) and x=13.8 (Panel C). Total visible extent is ~14 cm plus axis label text extending slightly beyond. This fits within 17 cm but is tight.
- Panel A y-axis labels are placed at x=−0.08 with `anchor=east`, and x-axis labels at y=−0.12 with `anchor=north`. Panel C bars have two-row x-axis labels at y=−0.12 and y=−0.42 (lines 1390–1406), which extend 0.42 cm below the baseline with no reserved space.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1459–1548 — `fig:survey-likert` (horizontal stacked bars, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- Q-labels are placed at x=−0.12 with `anchor=east`, style `qlbl`. Labels like "Q2: Tokenizer acc." and "Q5: \texttt{/compaction}" have non-trivial text widths that extend into negative x territory. TikZ's bounding box for the picture will include this leftward protrusion, which can shift the overall figure placement or cause overflow at the left margin if the figure is already constrained.
- The x-axis extends to x=10.3 (line 1478) and mean-value labels appear at x up to 8.15. Total right extent is ~10.3 cm. With the leftward label protrusion, the effective picture width is ~11–12 cm.
- No `\resizebox`.

---

**Lines 1578–1629 — `fig:survey-means` (horizontal bars, `\begin{figure*}`)**

- Q-labels at x=−0.12 with `anchor=east` (same issue as `fig:survey-likert`): labels like "Q6: Token awareness", "Q8: Install ease", "Q9: Dashboard clarity" extend into negative x space.
- Mean-value labels (`meanlbl` style, `anchor=west`) are placed immediately to the right of each bar end. The widest bar ends at x=8.10 (Q6), and the label "4.50" is at x=8.15. Additional tick labels at x=9.0 are placed at x=9.0 (line 1591). Total right extent ~9.5 cm. Tight but likely OK.
- No `\resizebox`.

### 5. Figures Using Suboptimal Relative Sizing

**Line 460 — `fig:dashboard` (`\begin{figure*}`)**
```
\includegraphics[width=0.52\textwidth]{tokalator-ui.png}
```
`0.52\textwidth` in a `figure*` environment means the image occupies only 52% of the full two-column text width, leaving 24% white space on each side after centering. For a screenshot used as a principal software demonstration figure, this will appear noticeably small. Compare to `fig:arch` (line 240, `0.88\textwidth`) and `fig:marketplace` (line 817, `0.92\textwidth`), which are more appropriate. `width=0.75\textwidth` or wider would be more consistent.

### 6. Caption Placement Inconsistency (three tables)

In `cas-dc` and most journal styles, table captions are placed **above** the tabular content. The majority of tables in this document follow that convention (captions at lines 150, 182, 702, 1294, 1416, 1637, 1657, 1707). This is not a sizing problem per se, but it is a formatting inconsistency that many journal style files (including `cas-dc`) treat as an error in the context of tables.

The web platform's library layer (\texttt{lib/pricing}, \texttt{lib/caching}, \texttt{lib/conversation}, \texttt{lib/context}) provides the computational backend for all seven calculators. The VS~Code extension maintains its own embedded model profiles and tokenizer logic (\texttt{modelProfiles.ts}, \texttt{tokenizerService.ts}) because it runs inside the extension host process and cannot import Next.js modules. Both implementations track the same provider pricing but are maintained independently. The extension's internal architecture follows a five-layer design:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textit{Core Engine} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}): subscribes to VS~Code editor events (active editor changes, tab open/close, document edits, diagnostic updates), builds \texttt{ContextSnapshot} records, and manages pinned files and model selection via \texttt{workspaceState}. All event handlers are debounced (300\,ms) to avoid performance overhead from rapid event firing.
  \item \textit{Tokenizer Service} (\texttt{tokenizerService.ts}): provider-specific BPE tokenizers, \texttt{claude-tokenizer} for Anthropic, \texttt{js-tiktoken} (\texttt{o200k\_base}) for OpenAI, heuristic ($\sim$4~chars/token) for Google. Tokenizers are lazy-loaded on first use and results are cached per-document keyed by URI and document version, so re-tokenization occurs only when the file changes.
  \item \textit{Relevance Scorer} (\texttt{tabRelevanceScorer.ts}): scores each open tab $R \in [0, 1]$ based on five weighted signals: language match ($+0.25$), import analysis ($+0.30$), path similarity ($+0.20$), edit recency ($+0.15$), and diagnostic count ($+0.10$). Pinned and active tabs are overridden to $R = 1.0$.
  \item \textit{Context Optimizer} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}, method \texttt{optimizeTabs()}): closes low-relevance tabs ($R < 0.3$) to free up context budget. The \texttt{/optimize} command identifies distractor tabs and closes them.

\end{itemize}

\begin{abstract}
AI-assisted coding environments operate within finite context windows of 128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens (as of early 2026). Although providers continue to expand these limits, the core problem remains: when developers open many files, model attention becomes diluted and API costs increase quadratically with conversation length, yet developers lack tools to monitor or control their token consumption.  Tokalator is an open-source context engineering toolkit with four components: (1) a VS Code extension that monitors token budgets in real time, scores open tabs by syntactic relevance across five signals, closes distractor tabs on demand, and provides an interactive chat participant with 11 commands; (2) a web platform with seven interactive calculators based on Cobb–Douglas quality modeling, caching break-even analysis ($n^* = 2$ for Anthropic models), and three conversation cost strategies with formal $O(T^2)$ cost proofs; (3) a reusable catalog of over 146 agents, 140 prompts, and 161 instruction files; and (4) a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and CLI that brings real Claude BPE token counting to Claude Code via stdio transport. %% UPDATE [v3.1.2]: "15 models" is wrong — modelProfiles.ts has 14 (4+7+3). Fix to "14 models" here and everywhere in the paper (abstract, highlights, comparison table, conclusions).
The toolkit covers \hl{14 models} from three providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google), is validated by 124 unit tests, and was introduced to over 220 developers through three community sessions and the VS Code Marketplace (\hl{77.62\% conversion rate, 163 acquisitions as of March~8, 2026}). %% RISKY CLAIM: "Most study participants... changing their tab management habits" —
%% "most" implies >50% but no formal survey or behavioral measurement backs this.
%% "Changing habits" is a behavioral outcome claim; self-reported intent ≠ actual behavior

---
name: tokalator-context-management
description: Real-time token budget awareness for AI coding sessions. Use Tokalator MCP tools to count tokens, estimate budget, preview turn cost, and avoid context overflow.

metadata:

  version: 1.0.0

# Tokalator Context Management

A skill for managing token budgets during AI coding sessions using the Tokalator MCP server. Gives agents real-time awareness of context usage, turn cost, and overflow risk — backed by real Claude BPE tokenizers, not guesses.

## Requirements

Tokalator MCP server must be running. Install it once:

```bash
# From the tokalator-mcp/ directory
npm install && npm run build
claude mcp add --transport stdio tokalator -- node tokalator-mcp/build/index.js
```

Verify with `/mcp` in Claude Code — `tokalator` should be listed.

## Available MCP Tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `count_tokens` | Count tokens in a text string for a given model |
| `estimate_budget` | Estimate token budget across one or more files |
| `preview_turn` | Preview token cost of the next conversation turn |
| `list_models` | List all supported models with context windows |

## When to Apply This Skill

Use Tokalator tools proactively in these situations:

- **Session start** — Run `estimate_budget` on the main files you'll work with to know your baseline
- **Before large reads** — Before reading a big file, use `count_tokens` to check if it fits comfortably
- **Mid-session check** — After several back-and-forth turns, run `preview_turn` to see how close you are to the limit
- **Before attaching files** — Check token cost before including large context in a prompt
- **Warning signs** — If responses feel compressed or context seems stale, check budget immediately

## Rules

### count_tokens

Call `count_tokens` before loading unknown-size content:

```
count_tokens(text: "<file contents or prompt text>", model: "claude-opus-4-6")
```

- Use the actual model being used in the session (default: `claude-opus-4-6`)
- If a file is over 50,000 tokens, warn the user before proceeding
- For files over 100,000 tokens, strongly recommend summarizing instead of reading in full

### estimate_budget

Call `estimate_budget` at session start and when switching task focus:

```
estimate_budget(files: ["src/main.ts", "src/utils.ts"], model: "claude-opus-4-6")
```

- Run on all files you plan to read or edit in the current task
- Report the total estimate to the user if it exceeds 30% of the context window
- If files + conversation overhead would exceed 70%, recommend narrowing scope

### preview_turn

Call `preview_turn` before sending a turn that includes large amounts of context:

```
preview_turn(currentTokens: <current usage>, model: "claude-opus-4-6")
```

- Run when turn count exceeds 15 (approaching context rot territory)
- Run before any turn that attaches 3+ files
- If `percentAfterTurn` exceeds 80%, warn the user and suggest compaction or a fresh session
- If `percentAfterTurn` exceeds 90%, halt and recommend starting a new session

### list_models

Call `list_models` when the user asks about or switches models:

```
list_models()
```

- Use this to confirm context window size before planning a large task
- Remind the user that Claude Opus 4.6 has a 1M token window, Sonnet 4.5 has 200K

## Context Rot Thresholds

Context rot occurs when too many turns accumulate stale context. Per-model rot thresholds:

| Model | Rot Threshold |
|---|---|
| claude-opus-4-6 | 40 turns |
| claude-sonnet-4-5 | 30 turns |
| claude-haiku-4-5 | 25 turns |
| gpt-5.2 / gpt-5.1 | 30 turns |
| o3 / o4-mini | 20 turns |
| gemini-3-pro | 30 turns |

When turn count approaches the rot threshold, suggest the user start a new session or use `/compact` to summarize.

## Budget Health Levels

| Level | Usage | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Healthy | < 60% | No action needed |
| Warning | 60–85% | Recommend closing unused context, summarizing |
| Critical | > 85% | Strongly recommend compaction or new session |

## Quick Reference

**Check if a file is safe to read:**
```
count_tokens(text: <file content>, model: "claude-opus-4-6")
→ If > 80,000 tokens: warn, consider summarizing
```

**Baseline at session start:**
```
estimate_budget(files: [<task files>], model: "claude-opus-4-6")
→ If > 30% of window: flag to user
```

**Mid-session health check:**
```
preview_turn(currentTokens: <used>, model: "claude-opus-4-6")
→ If percentAfterTurn > 80%: recommend compaction
```

**What model am I using?**
```
list_models()
→ Match to active Claude model for accurate context window
```

name: context-engineering
description: Context engineering expertise for AI-assisted development — token budgeting, context window management, caching strategies, and agent orchestration patterns.
user-invokable: true

# Context Engineering Skill

You are a context engineering expert. Apply these principles when helping with AI-assisted development tasks.

## Core Principles

### Token Budget Awareness
- Every token in the context window has a cost — both financial and attentional
- Input tokens are typically 3-5x cheaper than output tokens
- The practical attention budget is often smaller than the raw context window limit
- Always prefer the smallest set of **high-signal tokens** that maximize correct output

### Context Window Management
- **Progressive Disclosure**: Load context just-in-time rather than all at once
- **Lightweight Identifiers**: Maintain file path references and load content only when needed
- **Distractors**: Actively filter files that are topically related but don't contain the answer
- **Context Rot**: Monitor conversation length — accuracy degrades as tokens accumulate

### Memory Strategies (by scenario)

| Scenario | Strategy | Trade-off |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| Short tasks | **Trimming (Last-N)** — keep recent turns, drop old ones | Fast but loses early context |
| Long sessions | **Summarisation** — condense history into executive summary | Preserves big picture, loses detail |
| Precision work | **Context Editing** — remove stale tool results and thinking tokens | Up to 84% reduction, keeps flow |
| Cross-session | **Memory Tool / Copilot Memory** — persist facts externally | Eliminates cold-start problem |
| API-level | **Automatic Compaction** — SDK summarizes at token threshold | Transparent, 50-60% reduction |

### Caching Optimization
- Prompt caching reduces repeated prefix costs by ~90%
- Cache writes cost ~25% more than standard input
- Calculate break-even point: `cache_write_overhead / (standard_price - cache_read_price)`
- System prompts and stable prefixes are ideal cache candidates

### Agent Orchestration Patterns
- **Subagent isolation**: Delegate subtasks to agents with dedicated context windows
- **Parallel execution**: Run independent subtasks simultaneously across subagents
- **Specialization**: Use different models optimized for each role (planning vs. coding vs. review)
- **Agent hooks**: Enforce deterministic quality checks at lifecycle points (PreToolUse, PostToolUse)

## When to Apply

Apply this skill when:
- Planning multi-file changes that need context budgeting
- Optimizing prompts or instructions for token efficiency
- Designing agent workflows with multiple specialized agents
- Evaluating caching strategies for repeated API calls
- Diagnosing context rot or degraded output quality in long sessions
- Setting up agent skills, hooks, or orchestration patterns

## Guidelines

1. **Measure before optimizing** — use token counting to identify the largest context consumers
2. **Structure prompts with XML tags** — `<background>`, `<constraints>`, `<tool_guidance>` improve parsing
3. **Pin critical files** — mark essential files to survive compaction
4. **Set context rot warnings** — alert when conversation approaches degradation thresholds
5. **Use skills for domain expertise** — package reusable knowledge in SKILL.md files
6. **Configure agent hooks** — enforce linting, security checks, or formatting after tool calls

\subsection*{A.5.6 \quad Representative Verbatim Quotes}

The following quotes are drawn verbatim from survey open-text responses (lightly edited for grammar; participant IDs assigned sequentially by submission order; gender noted from the self-identification field):

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item[\textbf{P07}~(F)] \textit{``/preview showed me my system prompt was eating 4,800 tokens every single turn. I had no idea. I cut it by 60\% and my daily API cost dropped noticeably.''} (\textit{T1 / Q1})
  \item[\textbf{P14}~(M)] \textit{``I'm writing Turkish comments in my code. The 4-char heuristic said 1,200 tokens but the API said 1,580. That's a 32\% error, which matters when I'm near the limit.''} (\textit{T2 / Q2})
  \item[\textbf{P19}~(N-B)] \textit{``I appreciated having the token count visible without opening a browser tab. Even knowing \emph{roughly} how many tokens I'm using changed how I approach large refactoring tasks.''} (\textit{Q6})
  \item[\textbf{P23}~(M)] \hl{\textit{``I switched from GPT~5.3 to Claude Opus~4.6 mid-session and Tokalator still showed the GPT~5.3 window size. It took me a minute to realise why the budget numbers looked wrong.''}} (\textit{T3 / Q3})
  \item[\textbf{P31}~\hl{(M)}] \hl{\textit{``Every time I switched tabs, my pinned files would quietly un-pin themselves. I kept re-pinning the same three files before every session. Once the March~6 fix landed it just worked — pins survived across tab switches without me touching anything.''} (\textit{T4 / Q4})}
  \item[\textbf{P38}~\hl{(M)}] \textit{``Installation was painless — two minutes from Marketplace to first token count. That's exactly what a dev tool should feel like.''} (\textit{Q8})
  \item[\textbf{P42}~\hl{(M)}] \textit{``/compaction told me I'd hit the threshold in 4 more turns. That was actually useful. But I couldn't tell if it was my open files or the conversation that was growing fastest.''} (\textit{T5 / Q5})
  \item[\textbf{P48}~(M)] \textit{``I use SSH into a Linux container, so the VS Code extension isn't available. The \texttt{tokalator budget} CLI was the only way I could check my context. Please keep investing in it.''} (\textit{T1 / Q6})
\end{itemize}

%% ── A.5.7 Coding Protocol ─────────────────────────────────────────
\subsection*{A.5.7 \quad Coding Protocol}

Open-text responses were independently coded by the first author using an inductive open-coding approach~\cite{strauss1990basics}. A second pass consolidated overlapping codes into the five top-level themes. Inter-coder reliability was not formally measured (single coder); a limitation acknowledged in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}. No personally identifying information was collected; the survey form collected only self-identified gender, recruitment source, and free-text responses to each prompt. Participant IDs are sequential submission numbers assigned at export time.
